events/holy-synod-russia-1721/title: Peter the Great abolishes the Russian patriarchate
events/holy-synod-russia-1721/summary: Peter's Spiritual Regulation replaced the patriarch with a Holy Synod supervised by a lay Ober-Procurator, modelled on Protestant state consistories. The Russian church remained under this system until 1917.
events/holy-synod-russia-1721/consequenc: State control of Russian Orthodoxy for two centuries
events/melkite-schism-1724/title: Disputed patriarchal election divides the Church of Antioch
events/melkite-schism-1724/summary: On the death of Patriarch Athanasius III Dabbas, the pro-Catholic party in Damascus elected Cyril VI Tanas, while Constantinople consecrated the Athonite monk Sylvester. Rome recognised Cyril in 1729; his followers became the Melkite Greek Catholic Church and Sylvester's the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch.
events/melkite-schism-1724/causes/0: Decades of Catholic missionary activity in Aleppo and Damascus
events/melkite-schism-1724/causes/1: Rivalries between Damascus and Aleppo elites
events/melkite-schism-1724/consequences/: Two Byzantine-rite churches in the Antiochian patriarchate
Melkite civil recognition by the Ottomans (1848)
events/moravian-herrnhut-revival-1727/su: Refugees from Moravia, heirs of the Unity of Brethren, settled on Count Zinzendorf's estate at Herrnhut. After quarrels, a communion service on 13 August 1727 produced a powerful sense of the Spirit's unity; a hundred-year round-the-clock prayer watch and worldwide missions followed from 1732.
events/moravian-herrnhut-revival-1727/co: Moravian missions to the Caribbean, Greenland, South Africa
events/moravian-mission-st-thomas-1732/t: Moravian mission to enslaved Africans on St Thomas
events/moravian-mission-st-thomas-1732/s: Leonhard Dober and David Nitschmann sailed from Herrnhut to the Danish West Indies to preach to enslaved Africans — the first Protestant mission to the enslaved. Under Friedrich Martin, Afro-Caribbean congregations formed with Black helpers such as Rebecca Protten.
events/moravian-mission-st-thomas-1732/c: Herrnhut revival and Zinzendorf's missionary vision
events/first-great-awakening-1734/summar: Revival began under Jonathan Edwards in Northampton (1734–35) and swept the American colonies with George Whitefield's open-air preaching tours (1739–41), paralleling awakenings in Wales, Scotland and England. Converts testified to the 'new birth'; critics deplored emotional excess, splitting churches into New and Old Lights.
events/aldersgate-1738/summary: On 24 May 1738, hearing Luther's preface to Romans read at a Moravian society meeting, John Wesley felt his 'heart strangely warmed' and received assurance that Christ had taken away his sins. Within a year he took to field preaching and organised the Methodist societies.
events/aldersgate-1738/causes/0: Wesley's spiritual struggles and Moravian influence
events/chinese-rites-final-ban-1742/titl: Ex quo singulari bans the Chinese Rites
events/chinese-rites-final-ban-1742/summ: Benedict XIV’s bull Ex quo singulari confirms Clement XI’s condemnations (1704, 1715) of Chinese ancestral and Confucian rites and of the terms Tian and Shangdi for God, and imposes an oath on missionaries; Omnium sollicitudinum (1744) does the same for the Malabar Rites in India. Pius XII lifts the ban in 1939 (Plane compertum est).
events/chinese-rites-final-ban-1742/caus: Dominican and Franciscan objections to Jesuit accommodation
events/chinese-rites-final-ban-1742/cons: Kangxi’s and Yongzheng’s restrictions on Christianity
Weakening of the China mission until the 19th century
events/lisbon-earthquake-1755/summary: On All Saints’ Day 1755 an earthquake, tsunami and fire destroyed much of Lisbon, killing tens of thousands, many of them at Mass. Voltaire’s Poem on the Lisbon Disaster (1756) and Candide (1759) used it to mock Leibnizian optimism, and it became a turning point in debates about providence and natural evil.
events/lisbon-earthquake-1755/consequenc: Spurred naturalistic explanations of earthquakes (Kant, Pombal’s surveys)
events/philokalia-published-1782/summary: Nikodemos the Hagiorite and Makarios of Corinth compiled the Philokalia, an anthology of hesychast texts from the 4th to 15th centuries, printed in Venice. Paisius Velichkovsky's Slavonic version (1793) fuelled a Russian revival of eldership (startsy) and the Jesus Prayer.
events/korean-catholic-church-1784/summa: Korean scholars studying Catholic books from China sent Yi Seung-hun to Beijing, where he was baptised in 1784; on returning he baptised others, founding a church without missionaries. Repeated persecutions (1791, 1801, 1839, 1866) produced thousands of martyrs, including Andrew Kim Taegon (1846).
events/korean-catholic-church-1784/cause: Silhak scholars' interest in Western learning
events/first-service-in-sydney-1788/summ: The Anglican chaplain Richard Johnson held the first Christian service in Australia on 3 February 1788 for the convicts and marines of the First Fleet. Christianity in Australia began as a chaplaincy to a penal colony, while Aboriginal peoples experienced dispossession.
events/first-service-in-sydney-1788/cons: Anglican, Catholic and Protestant churches of Australia
events/episcopal-church-constituted-1789: General Convention constitutes the Episcopal Church

After American independence, Samuel Seabury was consecrated bishop by Scottish nonjuring bishops in Aberdeen (1784), and William White and Samuel Provoost by English bishops (1787). The General Convention of 1789 in Philadelphia adopted a constitution and an American Book of Common Prayer for the Protestant Episcopal Church in the United States.
American Revolution and the end of the Church of England's colonial role
Need for bishops without an oath to the British crown
First autonomous Anglican church outside the British Isles
Model of synodical government with lay participation
events/baptist-missionary-society-1792/s: Inspired by William Carey's Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens, Particular Baptist ministers founded a missionary society at Kettering. Carey sailed for India in 1793; the BMS inaugurated the age of voluntary Protestant mission societies.
events/baptist-missionary-society-1792/c: Carey's argument from the Great Commission
LMS (1795), CMS (1799) and many more societies
events/freetown-nova-scotian-settlers-17: About 1,100 Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia — many Baptist, Methodist and Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion Christians — sailed to Sierra Leone and founded Freetown, arriving singing hymns. Freetown became the base for West African Christianity, later home to recaptives like Samuel Ajayi Crowther.
American Revolution and British promises of freedom
First Protestant churches in West Africa led by Africans
events/tahiti-lms-mission-1797/summary: The ship Duff landed thirty London Missionary Society artisans and ministers at Matavai Bay. After years of hardship, chief Pōmare II converted (1812), and Tahitian and other Islander evangelists carried Christianity across Polynesia, often faster than European missionaries.
events/tahiti-lms-mission-1797/consequen: Islander missionaries to Samoa, Fiji and beyond
events/second-great-awakening-1800/summa: A prolonged wave of revivals in the early United States, from frontier camp meetings to Charles Finney's urban campaigns, made Methodists and Baptists the largest denominations and spawned reform movements — temperance, abolition, missions — and new religious bodies.
events/second-great-awakening-1800/conse: Restorationist and new movements, including Adventism and Latter-day Saints
events/serampore-mission-1800/summary: William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward settled in Danish Serampore, establishing a press that printed Scripture in some 40 Indian and Asian languages, a college (1818) and schools. Carey's opposition to sati contributed to its abolition (1829).
events/serampore-mission-1800/causes/0: East India Company hostility to missionaries in British territory
events/cane-ridge-revival-1801/summary: In August 1801 perhaps 10,000–20,000 people gathered at Cane Ridge for a week-long Presbyterian communion that became a revival with Methodist and Baptist preachers; many fell, jerked or shouted. Barton Stone, its host, later helped found the Restoration Movement.
events/abolition-slave-trade-1807/summar: After a twenty-year campaign led in Parliament by the evangelical William Wilberforce, with Quakers, the Clapham Sect and formerly enslaved writers like Olaudah Equiano, Britain outlawed the Atlantic slave trade. Slavery itself was abolished in the British Empire in 1833.
events/morrison-arrives-canton-1807/titl: Robert Morrison begins Protestant mission in China
events/morrison-arrives-canton-1807/summ: Robert Morrison of the London Missionary Society arrived in Canton, working for the East India Company as translator. He completed a Chinese Bible (1823) with William Milne and a Chinese–English dictionary, but baptised only a handful of converts.
events/marsden-new-zealand-1814/title: Samuel Marsden preaches in New Zealand
events/marsden-new-zealand-1814/summary: On Christmas Day 1814, Samuel Marsden preached on Luke 2:10 at Oihi with the support of the Ngāpuhi chief Ruatara, who translated. Māori conversion grew rapidly from the 1830s, often led by Māori evangelists, and Christianity shaped the Treaty of Waitangi (1840).
events/ame-church-founded-1816/summary: After being pulled from their knees in St George's Methodist Church, Richard Allen and Black Methodists founded Bethel Church and, in 1816, the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first independent Black denomination in the United States.
events/ame-church-founded-1816/consequen: AME missions in Africa and the Caribbean
events/prussian-union-1817/summary: For the 300th anniversary of the Reformation, King Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia, himself Reformed while most subjects were Lutheran, called for Lutheran and Reformed congregations to unite in one Evangelical church; a common agenda (liturgy) followed in 1822. Friedrich Schleiermacher supported union in principle while criticising royal control of worship.
events/prussian-union-1817/causes/1: Enlightenment and Pietist weariness with confessional division
events/prussian-union-1817/consequences/: Union churches in Prussia and other German states
Resistance and emigration of 'Old Lutherans' to North America and Australia
Basis of today's member churches of the EKD and the Union of Evangelical Churches
events/hawaii-mission-1820/summary: Missionaries of the American Board arrived months after the abolition of the kapu system; Queen Kaʻahumanu became a Christian and promoted the faith. Missionaries created a written Hawaiian language, schools and churches, and some descendants later joined the economic elite that overthrew the monarchy (1893).
